subject: Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.
posts:
Billions spent, yet the green slime returns. Vermont's Lake Champlain cleanup faces a wall of oversight gaps and budget shortfalls.
Evidence: EPA warnings, missing audits, rising costs
#LakeChamplain #Environment #Vermont

Vermont launched an ambitious 2015 initiative to clean waterways and meet tough EPA standards, promising a restored, swimmable Lake Champlain for everyone.
Stated Judgement: (+1.00, +1.00) — Greater Good

After spending nearly a billion dollars, the EPA warns Vermont is off track. Without proper audits or stable funding, toxic algae blooms persist.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.80, +0.90) — Greater Good

Verdict: PASS — Small Fall from Grace.
Well-meaning environmental goals collapsed into bureaucratic stagnation and missing oversight.

Integrity: Meaningful Distortion (Hypocrisy: 4.2, z: 2)
Vermont committed to clean Lake Champlain in 2015, but a decade later, cyanobacteria blooms continue to close beaches and threaten drinking water for 200,000 residents.

The Bright Side:
Dedicated local volunteers like Jeff van den Noort step up to monitor water quality, filling crucial data gaps left by lagging state oversight.
Plane Error: Confusing stated legislative ambition (Q4 Lyrical) with audited physical outcomes (Q3 Physical). Billions were spent without verifying tangible results.

Social Physics Analysis:
The state ran a well-intentioned initiative that devolved into administrative inertia. Without rigorous oversight, funding gaps crippled ecological goals.

The Trajectory: The Path of Small Fall from Grace.
Modal Dynamics: will be -> Won't be via Red Top.
Promising a restored lake while failing basic oversight creates a costly policy gap.

The Unavoidable Truth: Pouring money into environmental projects without strict oversight guarantees sluggish, incomplete results.
The Unavoidable Lie: Funding alone automatically equals ecological recovery.

Alethekanon:
Good intentions without rigorous institutional auditing produce expensive stagnation rather than ecological renewal.

Awwthekanon:
It breaks my heart to see community members testing toxic green sludge while millions vanish into bureaucratic black holes. Our waters deserve better care.

Brothekanon:
Bruh, a billion dollars down the drain and the algae is still thriving? Somebody needs to check the receipts on where that cash actually went.

Spirithekanon:
"Better a handful with quietness than both hands full, together with toil and grasping for the wind." Ecclesiastes 4:6 PASS
True stewardship requires careful wisdom, not merely throwing wealth at complex ecological crises.

Vermont Has Spent Nearly a Billion Dollars to Clean Up Lake Champlain. But the Green Slime Keeps Coming Back.

Vermont kicked off an ambitious effort in 2015 to clean up waterways and meet tougher EPA restrictions. But after a decade and nearly a billion dollars spent, potentially toxic algae still lingers in Lake Champlain. What happened?

On the last day of August, Jeff van den Noort spotted thick swirls of neon green film coating the water just steps from his home in Vermont. He waded in up to his ankles and dipped a jar to get a sample of the scum.

It wasn’t the first time he’d seen the slime. Since his parents bought the house on an island in Lake Champlain in 1966, van den Noort has spent part of nearly every summer in this quiet spot. Back then, the lake was clear.

But he began to witness the water’s deterioration as he grew older, especially after he moved into the home full time in 2010 to care for his ailing mother. That day in late August was the worst he’d seen all summer.

Later that week, van den Noort grabbed a bucket, a few Mason jars and a smartphone and got into his rusty Saab. He drove past the boat launches, frozen-in-time general stores and windswept pastures of the lake’s islands in northern Vermont and stopped at four other spots along the shore. Each time, he collected some murky water, gauged how thick the muck was, took a few photos and jotted down the weather conditions. He then uploaded his report to an online database.

Van den Noort was one part of a large volunteer effort to monitor a problem that has plagued Lake Champlain, which supplies drinking water to about 200,000 people. In recent decades, blooms of potentially toxic cyanobacteria, often called blue-green algae, have killed pets, forced beaches to close and hurt business and property values along the shores of this iconic Vermont feature.

“I just don’t feel like enough is being done,” van den Noort said. “And I think the state needs to take this seriously.”
